question:
Patient note:
A 53-year-old man presents early this morning to the ambulatory sports-medicine pre-operative suite for planned arthroscopic repair of a degenerative right rotator-cuff tear with subacromial decompression, an intervention the orthopedic surgeon estimates will require four portal sites and roughly ninety minutes of general anesthesia followed by a same-day discharge if pain control is adequate. He ambulated from the parking structure without assistance, climbed a flight of stairs to registration, and reports that until the shoulder pain worsened six months ago he regularly rode his bicycle ten miles each weekend; aside from avoiding overhead activities he remains fully mobile, walking his dog daily and performing all activities of daily living without aid. Two and a half weeks before today he completed a seven-day course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate prescribed by his primary physician after a chest radiograph confirmed a right lower-lobe community-acquired infiltrate; he never required hospitalization, intravenous antibiotics, or supplemental oxygen, and a follow-up phone call one week ago confirmed resolution of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic discomfort. He denies any episodes of systemic infection, rigors, or confusion since then, and he has not visited an emergency department or operating theatre in the past month. His medical history is otherwise notable for long-standing mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to a 20-pack-year smoking history; he quit eight years ago and now uses an albuterol metered-dose inhaler only before exertion, with no hospital admissions for respiratory exacerbations. Five years earlier, during an evaluation for an isolated prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time discovered on a routine insurance physical, hematology documented a circulating inhibitor that failed to correct with a 1:1 mix and produced a positive dilute Russell viper venom assay on two occasions twelve weeks apart; the consultant advised that the finding placed him at slightly increased thrombotic risk but did not prescribe chronic anticoagulation. He has never experienced calf tenderness, unilateral leg swelling, pleuritic chest pain, or unexplained shortness of breath suggestive of venous or pulmonary clot, and duplex ultrasonography has never been ordered. He also relates that prominent, tortuous blue superficial veins developed along the medial aspect of both calves during his early forties when he worked long shifts standing at an assembly line; the veins ache at day’s end but there is no skin discoloration, ulceration, or edema, and he occasionally wears 15–20 mm Hg compression socks for comfort. He has never worn a splint or cast, never fractured his hip, pelvis, or long bones, and has no history of spinal cord injury, stroke, myocardial infarction, inflammatory bowel disease, or cancer. He has never suffered congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism, or episodes of sepsis, and has not required hospitalization for any cardiac or systemic infectious process within the past month. Cardiac review of systems is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest tightness, or episodes of sudden weight gain. He takes no hormones, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet medications; his current regimen includes only albuterol as needed and a daily multivitamin. He drinks two beers on weekends, denies illicit drug use, and has maintained a body mass index of 27 kg/m². Physical examination finds an alert, well-nourished man seated comfortably. Temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class I, full cervical range of motion, and intact dentition. Breath sounds are vesicular with faint end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pulsation is 3 cm above the sternal angle. Abdomen is soft and nontender with active bowel sounds. Inspection of the lower limbs shows serpiginous dilated superficial veins along the great saphenous territory bilaterally; calf circumferences are equal at 38 cm, the skin is warm, there is no pitting, and gentle dorsiflexion elicits no tenderness. No vascular catheters, ports, or peripherally inserted central lines are present; a single 20-gauge peripheral IV was placed today in the left forearm. Neurologic screening reveals full strength and intact sensation in all extremities. Laboratory results obtained two hours ago demonstrate hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, hematocrit 45 %, platelets 242 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.5 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 20 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 38 s consistent with his known inhibitor; mixing study and specific factor assays are on file in prior records. A pre-operative electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 68 beats/min without conduction delay or ischemic change, and upright chest radiography performed after the recent pneumonia now demonstrates clear lungs and normal cardiac silhouette. Sequential compression sleeves have been ordered but remain off while final consent is obtained; no anticoagulant or antiplatelet agent has been given yet. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided an hour ago, and understands the operative plan, anticipated same-day discharge, and need for postoperative leg-pump use and early ambulation.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums weighted perioperative VTE risk factors present before surgery.
- One point each: age 53 (41–60), BMI 27 kg/m² (>25), visible varicose veins, COPD, and pneumonia within the past month. Subtotal = 5.
- Planned arthroscopic surgery = 2. The 90-minute duration does not earn a second procedure score.
- Documented lupus anticoagulant (persistent positive dilute Russell viper venom assay with an inhibitor pattern) = 3, even without prior thrombosis.
He remains mobile, has no prior VTE, and has only a peripheral IV, not a central venous catheter. No additional criteria apply.
Total: 5 + 2 + 3 = 10.
Final answer: 10
